title: Information capacity of quantum statistics: Fock-state tests of a discrete binary-sequence model on cloud photonic quantum processors
authors: Chiran Wijesundara, Octavia T. Volpe, Dejan Stojkovic, Herbert Fotso, Tim Thomay
abstract: Our central premise is that quantum mechanics may be the statistical limit of a more fundamental discrete theory: any such theory equips a physical system with a finite information capacity, and its departure from quantum statistics is controlled by how much of that capacity the system uses. We show that commercial cloud photonic quantum processors have reached the precision required to bound this capacity from below, using the binary-sequence model of Powers et al. as the concrete test theory: outcome probabilities arise from counting discrete sequences of length $n$, quantum mechanics is recovered as $n \to \infty$, and $n$ measures the information capacity of the register behind a prepared state. Photon Fock states $|1\rangle$, $|1,1\rangle$, heralded $|2\rangle$, and cascaded beam-splitter pairs are measured on programmable interferometers with dominant systematics determined in situ. The model's composition-consistent parametrization, singled out by requiring that rotations compose, recovers quantum mechanics with deviations $1.24/n$; a random-effects likelihood analysis calibrated by parametric bootstrap excludes all $n \le 100$: the information capacity of the register carrying the two-photon state, if finite, exceeds $10^2$. Cascaded beam splitters test the composition law directly: the data are split-invariant, excluding naive count composition at $8σ$ and confirming the interference-sign rule. Model-independently, curve-averaged deviations from the quantum partition law larger than $2.3\times10^{-2}$ are excluded at 95% CL, and the originally published linear parametrization is excluded outright. Because the compilation offset is frozen per circuit it is calibratable, opening the $10^{-3}$ floor ($n \sim 10^3$) to current hardware: cloud photonic processors are quantitative instruments for quantum foundations, and information capacity an experimentally boundable quantity.
summary: This work tests the hypothesis that quantum mechanics emerges as the statistical limit of a discrete underlying theory by measuring the information capacity of photonic quantum processors. Using the binary-sequence model, the authors set stringent bounds on this capacity, demonstrating that current hardware can experimentally constrain fundamental quantum principles. The results establish photonic processors as quantitative tools for quantum foundations research.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum mechanics is the statistical limit of a more fundamental discrete theory, which implies a finite information capacity for any physical system.
main_result: The experimental results bound the information capacity of the quantum register from below, showing it exceeds $10^2$, and confirming that the composition-consistent model is required to recover quantum mechanics.
method: The authors used random-effects likelihood analysis and differential tests on cloud photonic quantum processors to compare measured photon statistics against predictions from various discrete sequence models.
model_or_system: The physical system is a cloud photonic quantum processor using programmable interferometers to measure photon Fock states. The theoretical framework is the binary-sequence model of Powers et al., which relates outcome probabilities to counting discrete sequences of length $n$.
key_observables: Outcome probabilities, partition probabilities (e.g., $P(1, 1)$), and the deviation of measured statistics from the quantum partition law.
important_parameters: The information capacity $n$ (bounded below by $>100$), the deviation scaling factor ($1.24/n$), and the statistical floor ($1.1 	imes 10^{-3}$).
main_assumptions: Dominant systematics (like calibration offsets) are treated as nuisance parameters, and the analysis relies on the composition-consistent parametrization being the correct physical model.
figures_summary: Figures compare sequence-model vs. QM partition probabilities for $|2, 0angle$ input at $n=100$, show maximum deviation vs. $n$ for different model treatments, and illustrate the QM probability of forbidden outcomes falling as $n^{-4}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical premise (QM as a statistical limit), detailing the experimental setup on photonic processors, testing various discrete models (linear vs. composition-consistent), and finally deriving quantitative bounds on the information capacity.
why_interesting: It provides a direct, quantitative experimental test of the foundations of quantum mechanics by bounding a fundamental resource—information capacity—using state-of-the-art photonic quantum hardware.
